result.markdown: --- format: live-html: webr: packages: - survival --- # Matching in R {#sec-matchit} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## In this chapter **The question.** In Chapter 5 we matched a few patients by hand. How do we match the whole cohort in R, and how do we know whether the matching worked? **By the end of this chapter you will be able to:** - match patients with `matchit()`, using a caliper on the logit scale; - read the matching output, including how many patients were matched and dropped; - check balance with SMDs, Love plots and distribution plots, using cobalt; - extract the matched data, ready for the survival analysis in Chapter 7. ::: ## Warm-up: remember Chapter 5? {.unnumbered} Two quick questions to bring back the key ideas from last time. ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz([ { "q": "What does a caliper do in propensity score matching?", "options": [ "It sets the maximum distance allowed between the scores of two matched patients", "It decides which covariates go into the propensity score model", "It sets the number of controls for each treated patient", "It removes patients with missing data" ], "answer": 0, "why": "A treated patient with no control within the caliper is left unmatched, rather than being given a poor match.", "hints": [ "", "That's a modelling choice, made before matching.", "That's the matching ratio.", "Missing data are a separate issue." ] }, { "q": "Why are propensity scores compared on the logit (log-odds) scale when matching?", "options": [ "On the probability scale, scores near 0 and 1 are squashed together, so equal distances don't mean equally good matches", "Because logit scores are always positive", "Because the logit scale makes every patient match", "Because MatchIt can't use probabilities" ], "answer": 0, "why": "The logit scale spreads the scores out evenly, so a distance means the same thing everywhere.", "hints": [ "", "Logit scores can be negative: probabilities below 0.5 give negative logits.", "Matching on any scale can leave patients unmatched.", "MatchIt can use either scale. That's why the scale has to be set deliberately." ] } ]) ``` ## From hand matching to `matchit()` You'll need the simulated cohort from Chapter 5. Load it in the same way: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source("simulate_cohort.R") cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026) ``` ::: ## The workflow, and the tools {#sec-workflow} Putting it all together, a propensity score analysis has six steps: 1. **Specify** the confounders and the estimand. 2. **Estimate** the propensity score, usually by logistic regression. 3. **Match** treated to untreated patients with similar scores. 4. **Check balance** in the matched sample. If it's poor, go back to step 2 or 3, e.g. add interactions or squared terms, or change the caliper. *Don't look at outcomes* until the design is settled. 5. **Estimate** the treatment effect in the matched sample (@sec-together). 6. **Think about sensitivity** to unmeasured confounding. In Chapter 5 we did steps 2 and 3 by hand, to see how they work. In practice, you use two R packages: - **MatchIt** [@ho2011] does steps 2 and 3 in one function, `matchit()`. It fits the propensity score model, then matches using the method, ratio and caliper you choose. It returns the matched data, ready for analysis. - **cobalt** does step 4. It produces balance tables (`bal.tab()`) and plots, including the *Love plot* (`love.plot()`), which shows the SMD of each covariate before and after matching. ## Propensity score matching in R with `MatchIt` ### Steps 2–3: estimate the PS and match `matchit()` does what we did by hand in Chapter 5 (@sec-ps and @sec-matching). It fits the same logistic regression, then performs 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching without replacement, with a caliper of 0.2 SDs of the logit propensity score: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} m_out <- matchit( treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, # the PS model data = cohort, method = "nearest", # greedy nearest-neighbour matching distance = "glm", # propensity score from logistic regression ... link = "linear.logit", # ... with distances on the logit scale caliper = 0.2, # max distance: 0.2 SDs of the logit PS ratio = 1 # 1 control per treated patient ) m_out ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> A matchit object #> - method: 1:1 nearest neighbor matching without replacement #> - distance: Propensity score [caliper] #> - estimated with logistic regression and linearized #> - caliper: (0.169) #> - number of obs.: 2000 (original), 1428 (matched) #> - target estimand: ATT #> - covariates: age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output A summary of what was done: the matching method, how the propensity score was estimated ("linearized" means the logit scale), the **caliper** (0.169), and the number of patients before (2000) and after (1428) matching. **Watch the scale.** The caliper of 0.169 matches the value we calculated by hand in Chapter 5, because `link = "linear.logit"` puts it on the logit scale [@austin2011]. Without that argument, `matchit()` measures distances and the caliper on the *probability* scale. ::: ### Step 4: check balance with `summary()` and `cobalt` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(m_out, un = FALSE) # un = FALSE hides the pre-matching table ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Call: #> matchit(formula = treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, #> data = cohort, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", link = "linear.logit", #> caliper = 0.2, ratio = 1) #> #> Summary of Balance for Matched Data: #> Means Treated Means Control Std. Mean Diff. Var. Ratio eCDF Mean #> distance -0.1728 -0.2500 0.0936 1.1902 0.0239 #> age 66.4818 65.7983 0.0715 1.0372 0.0142 #> female 0.4300 0.4160 0.0285 . 0.0140 #> diabetes 0.2549 0.2213 0.0712 . 0.0336 #> bmi 28.6483 28.4917 0.0351 0.9791 0.0092 #> smoker 0.2619 0.2675 -0.0124 . 0.0056 #> eCDF Max Std. Pair Dist. #> distance 0.0854 0.0941 #> age 0.0700 0.8591 #> female 0.0140 1.0432 #> diabetes 0.0336 0.5284 #> bmi 0.0336 1.0055 #> smoker 0.0056 0.8480 #> #> Sample Sizes: #> Control Treated #> All 1151 849 #> Matched 714 714 #> Unmatched 437 135 #> Discarded 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output **Top table**: balance in the *matched* data, one row per covariate (`distance` is the propensity score itself). - **Means Treated / Means Control**: the group means after matching. For binary variables these are proportions. - **Std. Mean Diff.**: the SMD. **This is the column to check**: every value should be close to 0 (|SMD| < 0.1). - The other columns (`Var. Ratio`, `eCDF`, `Std. Pair Dist.`) compare other features of the distributions. You can leave them for now. **Sample sizes**: `All` is before matching. `Matched` is the patients kept. `Unmatched` is the patients left out, here 135 treated patients with no control within the caliper, plus the spare controls. ::: Every SMD is below 0.1, so the matching has balanced the measured covariates. A **Love plot** shows balance before and after matching at a glance. (It's named after the statistician Thomas Love, who popularised it, not after the emotion.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} love.plot(m_out, stats = "mean.diffs", abs = TRUE, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1), var.order = "unadjusted", colors = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2"), shapes = c("circle", "triangle")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Covariate balance before and after matching.](06-matching-in-r_files/figure-html/fig-love-1.png){#fig-love fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: Check the **overlap** of propensity scores, before and after: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} bal.plot(m_out, var.name = "distance", which = "both", type = "histogram", mirror = TRUE, colors = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution of propensity scores before and after matching.](06-matching-in-r_files/figure-html/fig-psdist-1.png){#fig-psdist fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: For continuous variables, check the whole distribution, not just the mean: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} bal.plot(m_out, var.name = "age", which = "both") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution of age in treated and control patients, before and after matching.](06-matching-in-r_files/figure-html/fig-balage-1.png){#fig-balage fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: ### Getting the matched data `match.data()` returns the matched sample. It has three extra columns: `distance` (the PS), `weights` (all 1 for 1:1 matching) and `subclass` (which pair each patient belongs to). We'll need `subclass` for the standard errors in Chapter 7. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} matched <- match.data(m_out) dim(matched) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 1428 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(matched[, c("id", "treated", "age", "diabetes", "distance", "weights", "subclass")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> id treated age diabetes distance weights subclass #> 1 1 0 70 0 -0.08309869 1 374 #> 3 3 0 66 0 -0.04388743 1 576 #> 5 5 0 58 1 0.19551254 1 54 #> 7 7 0 58 0 -0.20062921 1 7 #> 8 8 1 55 1 0.17718583 1 631 #> 9 9 1 66 0 -0.23877486 1 675 ``` ::: ::: ### Practice: fill in the blanks *This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.* The simulated `cohort` is already loaded. Replace each `______`, then click **Run Code**. (The first run downloads MatchIt and cobalt, so it takes a little longer.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_match'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_match for (pkg in c("MatchIt", "cobalt")) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(pkg, quiet = TRUE) } library(MatchIt) library(cobalt) simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) { set.seed(seed) age <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95)) female <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45) diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65))) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1) smoker <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25) lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) - 0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat)) lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes + 0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker shape <- 1.2 lambda <- 0.05 # baseline hazard scale (per year) t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape) t_admin <- runif(n, 3, 8) # study ends 3-8 years after entry t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04) t_cens <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout) time <- pmin(t_event, t_cens) status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens) data.frame( id = seq_len(n), age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker, treated, time = round(time, 3), status ) } cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match' caption='Practice: matching with MatchIt'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match #| caption: "Practice: matching with MatchIt" m <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "______", # measure distances on the logit scale caliper = ______) # 0.2 SDs of the logit propensity score # Sample sizes before and after matching summary(m, un = FALSE)$nn # Balance table: flag any |SMD| above 0.1 bal.tab(m, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = ______)) # Extract the matched data matched <- ______(m) nrow(matched) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_match"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 The logit-scale option is `"linear.logit"`. The caliper and the SMD threshold are numbers from this chapter: 0.2 and 0.1. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_match"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 The function that extracts the matched data is `match.data()`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_match"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r m <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2) summary(m, un = FALSE)$nn bal.tab(m, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1)) matched <- match.data(m) nrow(matched) ``` 714 treated patients were matched to 714 controls, so the matched data have 1428 rows. 135 treated patients had no control within the caliper. Every covariate is "Balanced, <0.1" after matching. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match #| check: true env <- .envir_result m <- env$m if (!inherits(m, "matchit")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Fill in the blanks in matchit() first, so that m is created.") } else if (!identical(m$info$link, "linear.logit")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use link = \"linear.logit\", so distances are measured on the logit scale.") } else if (length(m$caliper) == 0 || abs(m$caliper[[1]] - 0.1692) > 0.001) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "The caliper should be 0.2 (0.2 SDs of the logit propensity score).") } else if (!grepl("thresholds\\s*=\\s*c\\(\\s*m\\s*=\\s*0?\\.1\\s*\\)", .user_code)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "The SMD threshold in bal.tab() should be 0.1.") } else if (!is.data.frame(env$matched) || nrow(env$matched) != 1428) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Extract the matched data with match.data(m).") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! 714 treated patients matched to 714 controls (1428 rows), and every covariate is balanced (|SMD| < 0.1).") } ``` ::: :::: {.optional} ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Going further (optional): other matching and weighting options - `ratio = 2`: up to 2 controls per treated patient. More precise, but balance is sometimes a little worse. - `replace = TRUE`: controls can be reused. Better balance when good controls are scarce, but you need weights in the analysis. - `method = "optimal"` or `"full"`: optimal pair matching, or full matching (keeps everyone; can target the ATE). Needs the `optmatch` package. - `exact = ~ female`: force exact matches on key variables. - **Greedy vs optimal.** Greedy matching (the default) takes treated patients one at a time, so early choices can "use up" controls that would suit later patients better. Optimal matching minimises the *total* distance across all pairs. - **Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW)** with the `WeightIt` package: no one is discarded, and it targets the ATE by default. Check balance the same way with `cobalt`. - Use `distance = "gbm"` or other machine-learning PS models when the treatment model is complicated. **For more**, with worked examples of IPTW, matching with replacement, exact and full matching, and how to choose between them, see @sec-weighting. ::: :::: ## Quick quiz {.unnumbered} Choose an answer to each question. You'll get instant feedback and can change your answer as often as you like. ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz([ { "q": "Why do we set link = \"linear.logit\" in matchit()?", "options": [ "So distances and the caliper are measured on the logit scale, as recommended", "To fit a linear regression instead of a logistic one", "To match on the outcome", "It's needed to get a balance table" ], "answer": 0, "why": "Without it, matchit() measures distances (and the caliper) on the probability scale.", "hints": [ "", "The propensity score model is still logistic regression. Only the scale of the distances changes.", "The outcome never plays a part in matching.", "Balance tables work either way." ] }, { "q": "In summary(m_out), which column tells you whether matching balanced the covariates?", "options": [ "Std. Mean Diff.", "Means Treated", "eCDF Max", "Var. Ratio" ], "answer": 0, "why": "Check that every standardised mean difference is close to 0, ideally below 0.1 in absolute value.", "hints": [ "", "The means on their own don't show the size of the difference on a common scale.", "This compares distributions in a more technical way. Start with the SMDs.", "Variance ratios are a useful extra check, but the SMD is the main one." ] }, { "q": "What does the subclass column from match.data() record?", "options": [ "Which matched pair each patient belongs to", "Whether each patient was treated", "Each patient's propensity score", "Each patient's weight" ], "answer": 0, "why": "It identifies the matched pairs. Chapter 7 uses it for robust standard errors that allow for the pairing.", "hints": [ "", "That's the treated column.", "That's the distance column.", "That's the weights column." ] }, { "q": "A covariate was left out of the propensity score model. How can you check whether it is balanced after matching?", "options": [ "Add it with addl = in bal.tab()", "You can't check it", "Look at the propensity score histogram", "Refit the outcome model" ], "answer": 0, "why": "bal.tab(m, addl = ~ variable) reports balance on variables that weren't in the propensity score model.", "hints": [ "", "You can: cobalt checks balance on any variable in the data.", "Overlap of the scores doesn't tell you about a variable that isn't in the score.", "Balance is about the design, before any outcome model." ] } ]) ``` ## Exercise ### Exercise 6.1 The simulated `cohort` is already loaded in each box. Each part changes one matching choice and asks what happens. The parts are checked separately. #### Part 1: no caliper {.unnumbered} This is the matching from this chapter. **Remove the caliper**, then run it. How many treated patients are matched now, and how does balance compare? ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_match_nocal'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_match_nocal for (pkg in c("MatchIt", "cobalt")) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(pkg, quiet = TRUE) } library(MatchIt) library(cobalt) simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) { set.seed(seed) age <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95)) female <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45) diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65))) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1) smoker <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25) lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) - 0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat)) lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes + 0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker shape <- 1.2 lambda <- 0.05 # baseline hazard scale (per year) t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape) t_admin <- runif(n, 3, 8) # study ends 3-8 years after entry t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04) t_cens <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout) time <- pmin(t_event, t_cens) status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens) data.frame( id = seq_len(n), age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker, treated, time = round(time, 3), status ) } cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match_nocal' caption='Exercise 6.1, part 1: no caliper'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match_nocal #| caption: "Exercise 6.1, part 1: no caliper" m_nocal <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2) summary(m_nocal, un = FALSE)$nn bal.tab(m_nocal, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1)) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_match_nocal"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 Delete `, caliper = 0.2` from the `matchit()` call (keep the closing bracket). ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_match_nocal"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r m_nocal <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit") summary(m_nocal, un = FALSE)$nn bal.tab(m_nocal, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1)) ``` Without a caliper, all 849 treated patients are matched (there are more controls than treated patients, so everyone finds *someone*). But the matches for the high-scoring treated patients are poor, and balance is much worse: age (SMD 0.25), diabetes (0.29) and BMI (0.15) are all still above 0.1. Keeping everyone isn't worth it if the groups aren't comparable. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match_nocal' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match_nocal #| check: true m <- .envir_result$m_nocal if (!inherits(m, "matchit")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Keep the model's name, m_nocal.") } else if (length(m$caliper) > 0) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Remove the caliper argument from matchit().") } else if (!inherits(.result, "bal.tab")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the balance table the last line.") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! All 849 treated patients are matched, but age, diabetes and BMI now have |SMD| above 0.1. More patients, worse balance.") } ``` ::: #### Part 2: two controls per treated patient {.unnumbered} Keep the caliper, but allow up to **2** controls for each treated patient (see the optional box on other matching options). What happens to the sample size and the balance? ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_match_ratio'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_match_ratio for (pkg in c("MatchIt", "cobalt")) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(pkg, quiet = TRUE) } library(MatchIt) library(cobalt) simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) { set.seed(seed) age <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95)) female <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45) diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65))) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1) smoker <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25) lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) - 0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat)) lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes + 0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker shape <- 1.2 lambda <- 0.05 # baseline hazard scale (per year) t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape) t_admin <- runif(n, 3, 8) # study ends 3-8 years after entry t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04) t_cens <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout) time <- pmin(t_event, t_cens) status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens) data.frame( id = seq_len(n), age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker, treated, time = round(time, 3), status ) } cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match_ratio' caption='Exercise 6.1, part 2: ratio = 2'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match_ratio #| caption: "Exercise 6.1, part 2: ratio = 2" m_r2 <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2, ratio = ______) summary(m_r2, un = FALSE)$nn bal.tab(m_r2, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1)) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_match_ratio"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 `ratio = 2` allows up to two controls per treated patient. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_match_ratio"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r m_r2 <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2, ratio = 2) summary(m_r2, un = FALSE)$nn bal.tab(m_r2, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1)) ``` The same 714 treated patients are matched, now to 987 controls instead of 714, so the analysis would be more precise. R warns that not every treated patient found 2 controls within the caliper. Every covariate is still balanced (|SMD| below 0.1), though balance is slightly worse than with 1:1 matching: the SMD for age rises to 0.08, and the propensity score itself (`distance`) is just over the threshold, at 0.12. With a variable number of controls per patient, the matching **weights** are no longer all 1, so they must be used in the analysis (@sec-together). ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match_ratio' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match_ratio #| check: true m <- .envir_result$m_r2 if (!inherits(m, "matchit") || !isTRUE(m$info$ratio == 2)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Set ratio = 2 in matchit().") } else if (length(m$caliper) == 0) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Keep the caliper: caliper = 0.2.") } else if (!inherits(.result, "bal.tab")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the balance table the last line.") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! 714 treated patients are matched to 987 controls, and every covariate still has |SMD| below 0.1. Remember to use the weights in the analysis.") } ``` ::: #### Part 3: leave a confounder out {.unnumbered} **Remove `smoker`** from the propensity score model. Then check whether smoking is balanced after matching. Because `smoker` is no longer in the model, `bal.tab()` needs `addl = ~ smoker` to include it. Make the balance table the last line. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_match_nosmk'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_match_nosmk for (pkg in c("MatchIt", "cobalt")) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(pkg, quiet = TRUE) } library(MatchIt) library(cobalt) simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) { set.seed(seed) age <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95)) female <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45) diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65))) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1) smoker <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25) lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) - 0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat)) lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes + 0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker shape <- 1.2 lambda <- 0.05 # baseline hazard scale (per year) t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape) t_admin <- runif(n, 3, 8) # study ends 3-8 years after entry t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04) t_cens <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout) time <- pmin(t_event, t_cens) status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens) data.frame( id = seq_len(n), age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker, treated, time = round(time, 3), status ) } cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match_nosmk' caption='Exercise 6.1, part 3: leaving smoker out'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match_nosmk #| caption: "Exercise 6.1, part 3: leaving smoker out" m_nosmk <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2) bal.tab(m_nosmk, addl = ~ ______, binary = "std", un = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_match_nosmk"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 Delete `+ smoker` from the formula in `matchit()`. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_match_nosmk"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 Then `addl = ~ smoker` adds smoking to the balance table. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_match_nosmk"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r m_nosmk <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi, data = cohort, method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2) bal.tab(m_nosmk, addl = ~ smoker, binary = "std", un = TRUE) ``` The four variables in the model are balanced, but smoking isn't: its SMD is 0.16 after matching, slightly *worse* than the 0.14 before. Nothing in the matching made smoking balance. Because smoking affects survival, the treatment effect estimate would be confounded. This is the measured version of the unmeasured-confounding problem from @sec-app-psm. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_match_nosmk' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_match_nosmk #| check: true m <- .envir_result$m_nosmk if (!inherits(m, "matchit")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Keep the model's name, m_nosmk.") } else if ("smoker" %in% all.vars(m$formula)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Remove smoker from the propensity score formula.") } else if (!inherits(.result, "bal.tab") || !("smoker" %in% rownames(.result$Balance))) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line a balance table that includes smoking: addl = ~ smoker.") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Smoking is not balanced after matching (SMD 0.16, slightly worse than before). Leaving out a confounder means nothing balances it.") } ``` ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important icon="false"} ## Key points - `matchit()` estimates the propensity score and matches in one step. Use `link = "linear.logit"` so that distances and the caliper are on the logit scale. - The output shows how many patients were matched. Treated patients with no control within the caliper are dropped. Always report how many. - Check balance with `summary()` or `bal.tab()`: every |SMD| should be below 0.1. Love plots and distribution plots show the same thing visually. - `match.data()` returns the matched data, with `weights` and `subclass` (the matched pairs), ready for analysis. - Check balance **before** looking at any outcomes. ::: **Answering the question.** `matchit()` matched 714 treated patients to 714 controls. 135 treated patients had no control within the caliper. After matching, every covariate had |SMD| < 0.1, so the matched groups are comparable on all five measured confounders. Chapter 7 compares their survival. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {quiz} from "./js/survtools.js" ``` ## Further reading All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise.
